title: 2 Chronicles 30:1–12
context: After cleansing the temple in chapter 29, Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah, including the remnant of the northern tribes after the Assyrian conquest, to keep the Passover at Jerusalem. Because the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient numbers and the people had not gathered in time, the king and assembly decide to keep it in the second month, a timing the law allowed for those unclean or far away (Numbers 9:10–11). Couriers carry letters from Beersheba to Dan, calling the people to turn again to the LORD, who is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face if they return. Many mock the messengers, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humble themselves and come, while the hand of God gives Judah one heart to obey. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about God’s gracious invitation, repentance, and unity in worship, while they describe differently how God’s hand on the heart relates to the people’s response.

verses.text: Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the LORD’s house at Jerusalem, to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah inviting all Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. The invitation is wide and sincere, reaching even those from the fallen northern kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king gathering the scattered covenant people around the place God chose (compare Deuteronomy 12:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of renewed unity in worship.

verses.text: For the king had taken counsel with his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem to keep the Passover in the second month.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king taking counsel with his princes and the assembly to keep the Passover in the second month. Leaders seek a faithful way forward together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the decision as consistent with the law’s provision for a second-month Passover (compare Numbers 9:10–11). Both traditions commonly read the verse as wise, shared leadership.

verses.text: For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient number, and the people had not gathered themselves together to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient numbers and the people had not gathered in time. Honest assessment leads to a practical delay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the delay as reverent care that worship be rightly prepared. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as balancing zeal with readiness.

verses.text: The thing was right in the eyes of the king and of all the assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the plan as right in the eyes of the king and the assembly. Agreement among God’s people strengthens the reform.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared approval as a sign of God’s work in uniting his people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a brief note of consensus in a good cause.

verses.text: So they established a decree to make proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba even to Dan, that they should come to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it in great numbers in the way it is written.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the proclamation going from Beersheba to Dan, since the Passover had not been kept in great numbers as written. The call is to return to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the decree as restoring worship according to Scripture after long neglect. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as zeal for faithful obedience across the whole land.

verses.text: So the couriers went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah, according to the commandment of the king, saying, “You children of Israel, turn again to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may return to the remnant of you that have escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the couriers calling Israel to turn again to the LORD so that he may return to the remnant. The invitation is a genuine call to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise that God will return to those who return to him as grounded in his covenant faithfulness (compare James 4:8). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a gracious summons to the survivors of judgment.

verses.text: Don’t be like your fathers and like your brothers, who trespassed against the LORD, the God of their fathers, so that he gave them up to desolation, as you see.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the warning not to be like the fathers who trespassed and were given up to desolation. Past judgment serves as a real warning for present choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal to history as showing the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to learn from the failures of earlier generations.

verses.text: Now don’t be stiff-necked, as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD, and enter into his sanctuary, which he has sanctified forever, and serve the LORD your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call not to be stiff-necked but to yield to the LORD and serve him. The people are urged to respond freely and humbly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call to yield as an invitation that God’s grace makes effective in those who come. Both traditions commonly read the verse as urging humble submission so that God’s anger may turn away.

verses.text: For if you turn again to the LORD, your brothers and your children will find compassion with those who led them captive, and will come again into this land, because the LORD your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn away his face from you if you return to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the promise that the LORD is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from those who return. God’s mercy is freely offered to all who turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as echoing God’s revealed character (compare Exodus 34:6; Deuteronomy 30:2–3). Readers in both traditions commonly treat the verse as a strong encouragement to repentance.

verses.text: So the couriers passed from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, even to Zebulun, but people ridiculed them and mocked them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that many in Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun ridiculed and mocked the couriers. A sincere invitation can be refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the mockery as the sad but expected response of hardened hearts. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly as showing that not all who hear the call respond.

verses.text: Nevertheless some men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see some men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbling themselves and coming to Jerusalem. Humility opens the way to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these men as a remnant drawn by God’s grace. Readers in both traditions commonly celebrate those who humbled themselves amid widespread scorn.

verses.text: Also the hand of God came on Judah to give them one heart, to do the commandment of the king and of the princes by the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the hand of God giving Judah one heart to obey, and they commonly understand this as grace that enables and unites a willing people without overriding their response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same words as God’s own work in producing unity and obedience (compare Ezekiel 36:26). Both traditions commonly agree that the unity is God’s gift, while describing differently how his work relates to the people’s choice.
